title: Why Does Hosting Stress Us Out So Much?
summary:
In the year's biggest TV shows and movies, from 'The Odyssey' to 'The Invite,' hosting anxiety takes center stage.

The post Why Does Hosting Stress Us Out So Much? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
The pressure of hosting has weighed on humanity since the dawn of civilization.

Despite thousands of years of practice, if this summer’s film and streaming releases are to be believed, the practice of serving wine and spirits to guests is just as fraught as ever. From the panicked hosts in Olivia Wilde’s marital satire The Invite and Katie Dippold’s nautical horror comedy Widow’s Bay to the exploitative guests who eat and drink everything in sight in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, hosting anxiety is at the center of the cultural zeitgeist right now. 

Having people over is supposed to be fun, carefree, a way to fill one’s social cup. So why does it stress us out so much?

This could be coming up because the dinner party is in the midst of a revival. A 2025 study of 2,000 Americans found 72% of those surveyed prefer staying in with friends over going out, half of whom claim this shift occurred in the past few years. While two-thirds of respondents claimed they prefer the more comfortable environment (65%), 53% said hosting at home is a great way to save money—no surprise given the rising costs of just about everything. 

While hosting home gatherings lessens the economic burdens of having a social life, this shift comes with a new set of stressors. A quarter of those surveyed said they worry about making guests feel comfortable, running out of food or drinks, and feel pressure to make everything perfect—similar to what we’re seeing on the screen.

‘Get the Wine’ and ‘Serve the Punch Now.’ Like, Immediately

This pressure to be perfect hosts overwhelms The Invite’s protagonist, Angela, as well as Patricia in Widow’s Bay. In both, the expectation to dazzle guests with charm, wit, and booze weighs heavily on the women—despite the male protagonists showing little to no interest in their efforts.

The Invite sees struggling San Francisco married couple Angela (Wilde) and Joe (Seth Rogen) invite their eccentric, sexually-liberated upstairs neighbors, Piña (Penélope Cruz) and Hawk (Edward Norton), over for the first time. Misunderstandings (a k a marital fibs) lead to a table adorned with assorted cheeses, pickles, and jamón, but sans alcohol. Wilde’s painfully anxious character downs most of their sole bottle of Champagne before the couple arrives, making the only hope in wooing their guests with a sophisticated drink the 1980 anniversary Château Haut-Brion they’ve been saving for a special occasion. “Get the wine,” Angela tells Joe through gritted teeth. 

Angela, a bored housewife with a dusty fine arts degree, is a meditation on the stereotypical unsatisfied stay-at-home mom who seeks fulfilment in meticulous interior decoration and domestic planning—tending to a house that is never quite finished and planning a dinner party as if there’s a gun to her head. With no friends, no job, and a floundering marriage, Angela is painfully isolated, and her thirst for belonging drives her desperate attempts to impress her alluring neighbors.

In episode four of Widow’s Bay, Kate O’Flynn’s Patricia, the underappreciated middle-aged assistant to the uptight mayor (Matthew Rhys) of a Martha’s Vineyard-esque island, attempts to forge friendships—and validation—by planning a party called “Patricia’s Sunset Cocktails” with the help of a bizarre self-help book she found in a donations box. With a ‘50s trad wife aesthetic (patriarchal social norms and all), Your Turn: Out With the Old and in With the You is revealed to be a demonic book of spells and incantations posing as a guide that empowers timid female readers to change their lives by throwing the perfect party. With commands like “SERVE THE PUNCH NOW,” the grimoire’s increasingly authoritative tone reflects Patricia’s own anxiety as both a host and a woman worthy of connection in a world that has rejected her. Like Angela, Patricia is so anxious to impress she attempts to soothe her nerves by knocking down several cups of that potion “punch”—made from crow’s blood, feathers, and possibly rum. 

Though over the top, these characters epitomize the frazzled host who is chasing validation by way of the perfect party.

“Hosting brings a unique blend of logistical pressure and emotional responsibility, and for many it’s the perfect recipe for stress,” licensed counselor Elizabeth Bodett Dresser, LCPC explains to Real Simple. “From a psychological standpoint, hosting anxiety usually stems from a few familiar patterns: perfectionism, social comparison, and family dynamics. We want our homes, food, and behavior to reflect well on us, and we worry about being judged if things aren’t ‘just right.’”

Guests or Gods?

But hosting anxiety isn’t just about looking good for guests—there’s also the potential stress of not being able to get them to leave. According to that same 2025 survey, 15% of hosts worry about guests overstaying their welcome and 12% fret over managing different personalities and social dynamics—similar to what we see in The Odyssey.  

The concept of “Zeus’ Law” or xenia, the sacred ancient Greek code of hospitality, has always been central to Homer’s epic but is particularly pronounced in Nolan’s film. Zeus’ xenia concept is sometimes translated as “guest-friendship,” the rule commands hosts to generously feed and shelter any visitor, based on the belief that a stranger could be a god in disguise. Ironically, not abiding by the peaceful communal code of conduct could lead to “divine punishment” for the host.

Despite knowing she’s being taken advantage of by Antinous (Robert Pattinson), the controlling leader of the throng of 108 greedy suitors, Penelope (Anne Hathaway) is a model example of true xenia.

But is it right? Since the film debuted, the topic has been all over the internet. Greek scholar and translator Emily Wendt calls the suitors’ behavior “abusive xenia” in an Instagram video explaining the concept: “Why in The Odyssey does Penelope let these suitors, these hundreds of random men come and eat all her food? The host has to take care of the guest and it’s the guest’s duty to not abuse the kindness and generosity of the host.” 

Wendt also calls out the Cyclops called Polyphemus, the son of Poseidon, for being an awful host to Odysseus and his crew because he—please hold, just double-checking some notes— “smashes them and eats them.” (Talk about poor hospitality.) She notes that abusers of xenia are ultimately punished. “You have to have trust that if you show up somewhere at someone’s house and you have nowhere to sleep and you don’t have any food that they’re not going to kill you,” she says.

Perhaps due to his hero status, Odysseus seems to get a pass for being a bad guest; shooting Polyphemus’ sole eye on his way out is not exactly a classy way to exit a home.

While hosting etiquette predates the days of The Odyssey and Zeus’ law, in many ways what we see in the film is the classical origin of what is now considered good hospitality—i.e. treat others as you’d wish to be treated. When asked about its depiction throughout the film, Nolan told The New York Times, “for that world it’s very clearly basic survival.” 

And while there are commendable aspects to the bare bones of Zeus’ Law, the question remains: Is hosting always a matter of survival, social or otherwise? 

Let’s hope not.

title: How to Pair Wine with Fiery Sichuan Dishes
summary:
From Cava Rosado and mapo tofu to Savagnin and bang bang chicken, these expert pairings will bring a tear to your eye (and not just from the spice).

The post How to Pair Wine with Fiery Sichuan Dishes appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
There’s a persistent idea that the best wine to pair with “Asian food”—as if it’s a monolith—is a crisp and lightly sweet white wine.

To be fair, this is a fabulous option for simultaneously spicy, pungent, and umamirich flavors. But Sichuan food (and its three major styles, Shanghebang, Xiaohebang, and Xiahebang) is especially complex, and when confronted with a spread of dishes that balance fiery, sweet, sour, salty, pickled, and fermented ingredients, you may be baffled.

The goal is to focus on one “hero” dish and choose a wine flexible enough to go with everything.

Mapo Tofu with Cava Rosado

True mapo tofu is all about málà (or “numbing and spicy”), the trademark numbing sensation from Sichuan pepper, which is actually in the citrus family, unrelated to black or chili pepper. A sparkling wine provides a necessary cleansing sensation, but one that’s too crisp or dry will feel out of place against this rich dish that combines chili, fermented bean paste, and minced beef or pork. Enter Cava Rosado, which employs the same traditional-method production as white Cava but with skins of Garnacha, Monastrell, Pinot Noir, or Trepat to give it depth in both texture and flavor. These wines have a fine, almost creamy mousse and often a floral quality reminiscent of Sichuan pepper.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Agrupacio Viticultors Artesanals NV Castell de Sant Pau BRUT ROSE Grenache Blend (Cava)

Citrus and apricot blossom, fresh cherry and spice are carried by a creamy mousse into a crisp and persistent palate. Friendly, energetic, and a pleasure. Versatile at the table with anything from fresh seafood, grilled white meats, or richer risotto. 92 Points — Elaine Chukan Brown

$11 Mission Liquor

Juvé y Camps NV Brut Rose Pinot Noir Pinot Noir (Cava)

Vibrant cherry in the glass, this rosé showcases macerated cherries and berries, honeysuckle, and lightly toasted croissant. Energetic while full of flavor, this sparkling wine can accompany a range of dishes from seared tuna to risotto, Iberian ham to soft cheeses. 91 Points — E.C.B.

$17 Stirling Fine Wines

Kung Pao Chicken with Frappato

True Sichuan kung pao chicken doesn’t resemble the sweet peanuty versions of so many American takeout spots. Instead, it is defined by extremely spicy, dried red chili. Accordingly, don’t pair your wine with the peanuts or chicken, but rather with those chilies. Frappato, common in Sicily, is a red grape with intense aromas but a light body and low tannins that won’t clash with the heat. While dominated by red-berry flavors, it often shows complementary dried-chili notes, along with black tea and warming spices like cinnamon and clove, which are also common in Sichuan cooking. Try it with a slight chill, which will enhance its refreshing quality.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Arianna Occhipinti 2023 Il Frappato Frappato (Terre Siciliane)

On the nose, violets, wild cherries and wild strawberries pop above a backbone of pepper and crushed herbs. The palate has an incredible freshness, but also profundity. Frappato always feels especially connected to the earth, tethered to something deep underneath us. Arianna has a special talent for teasing out that sensation. 95 Points — Danielle Callegari

$40 Envoyer Fine Wines

Valle dell’Acate 2024 Il Frappato Frappato (Vittoria)

The nose is savory and herbaceous, but also features powerful currents of tangy red fruit and salinity. The palate is both sweet and salty, with flavors of orange peel and wild cherry, before the herbs and earth eventually return. Tannins are slick and polished, but with grip. 91 Points — D.C.

$26 Wine.com

Yúxiāng Shredded Pork with Arinto

Yúxiāng (or “fish flavor,” despite containing no fish) is a signature flavor profile of Sichuan cuisine. Garlic takes center stage (this dish is sometimes called pork in garlic sauce), enhanced with ginger, pickled chili, fermented bean, sugar, and vinegar. Though garlic can be tricky to pair with wine, most high-acid, unoaked whites work well, much like how lemon harmonizes with garlic in the kitchen. Arinto is a flagship white grape of Portugal, especially in the Vinho Verde region, with abundant citrus that goes not only with garlic, but also with ginger and pickled notes. Arinto also has a subtle saline quality that makes it especially good with salty and pungent dishes.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Quinta de Chocapalha 2022 Arinto (Lisboa)

Fruity old vine Arinto, with a crisp apple flavor and lively acidity, this is a fresh white wine ready to drink young. Its grassy aroma and vibrancy promise a delicious taste. Drink now. Best Buy. 90 Points — Roger Voss

$20 Wine.com

Quinta de Paços 2022 Casa de Paços Reserva Arinto (Minho)

This wine has irresistibly electric acidity and river stone minerality at its core, allowing the flavors of lime curd, tangerine zest, and roasted hazelnut to surge to the finish, where subtle notes of white pepper and butterscotch add to the complex package. Long and rather Chablis-esque in structure, this’ll be a dandy with baked halibut. Drink over the next 3-4 years. 92 Points — John Sumners

$20 Astor Wines & Spirits

Bang Bang Chicken with Savagnin

Guàiwèi (or “strange flavor”) is a Sichuan flavor that can be described as every taste sensation firing at once. “Bang bang” is sometimes used in U.S. restaurants for a very different dish, but the original is shredded poached chicken in a spicy sesame sauce, similar to the sauce for dan dan noodles, another Sichuan dish that has taken many detours. Savagnin, a white grape mostly found in Jura, has nutty notes even when not made in its popular oxidative style (non-oxidative styles are called ouillé, or “topped-up”), and like guàiwèi, many flavors coexist: amaretto, ripe pear, preserved lemon, wet stone. Either oxidative or ouillé styles do a bangup job here.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Rijckaert 2022 Grand Elevage Vieilles Vignes Savagnin (Arbois)

From old vines, this Savagnin is fruity while also dense. It has a bite of almonds and zesty acidity. That is allied to young fruitiness so the wine needs to age further. Drink from 2025. 91 Points — R.V.

$42 Hart & Cru

Domaine Dugois 2023 Auréoline Savagnin (Arbois)

Slightly oxidative, showing light nutty aromas and flavors alongside ripe overquince and orange peel. The palate is lively and vibrant, with bright acidity and a clean, focused finish. Balanced and intriguing, with subtle complexity and a distinctive character. 90 Points — Aleks Zecevic

$28 Sec Wines

title: Why Washington’s ‘Underdog’ Region Is Getting Winemakers Excited
summary:
With world-class Pinot Noir and cool-climate varietals, the Puget Sound AVA is becoming one of the country's most promising wine regions.

The post Why Washington’s ‘Underdog’ Region Is Getting Winemakers Excited appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Award-winning cool-climate Pinot Noir and Siegerrebe that sings of white flowers and tropical fruits? That’s not what comes to mind when you think “Washington State.” Yet the Puget Sound AVA—Washington’s only appellation west of the Cascade Mountains, spanning a 200-mile corridor north and south of Seattle—is evolving into one of the country’s most promising regions

Where the rest of Washington is arid and semi-arid continental desert, with barely six inches of rain in most years, this soggy waterfront stretch can get up to 10 times as much rain. On paper, it’s more like the nearby Willamette Valley, or parts of Galicia, Germany, and Western Loire. And like those regions, climate change is providing more opportunities than challenges.

“The Puget Sound growing season has been getting consistently warmer and drier over the years, and that shift is quietly turning this region into one of the most compelling places to grow Pinot Noir,” says Kimberly Harris of Bayernmoor Cellars, whose 2023 Estate Précoce Pinot Noir and 2023 Clone 777 Pinot Noir both earned 93 points from Wine Enthusiast. “The long, slow ripening that cool maritime air provides is still there, but we’re seeing more of the reliable sunshine and reduced rainfall that Pinot demands to reach its full potential. The region isn’t just good for Pinot anymore—it’s becoming ideal for it.”

While Pinot Noir is considered a star grape, variety rules the AVA. Bainbridge Vineyards grows 10 varieties, among them Agria, Dunkelfelder, and Garanoir; Perennial Vintners makes Zweigelt and Melon de Bourgogne; Skagit Crest has Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, and Sauvignon Blanc; San Juan Vineyard makes Rhône (GSM) and Bordeaux (Cab Franc and Sauv) blends; and Château NoElle has Izkorka, Auxerrois, and Pinot Gris among the many varieties planted on the western slope of the Cascade foothills. Some producers also grow hybrid grapes, such as Regent, Rondo, Golubok, and Marquette.

MOST WIDELY PLANTED GRAPES: Pinot Noir, Madeline Angevine, Siegerrebe
CLIMATE: Cool maritime climate shaped by Pacific Ocean airflows.
SOIL TYPES: Gravelly, sandy loam over glacial hardpan.

At Öömrang, Christine and Edmund Stoecklein make wines inspired by Germany’s Franken region, where Edmund’s family has made wine since the 1800s. They grow Siegerrebe, Müller-Thurgau, Kerner, and Sylvaner on 22 acres of their 85-acre farm. The farm-driven nature of the winemaking stands in stark contrast to the town of Woodinville, just east of Seattle, where over 100 producers make wine in a warehouse system with grapes grown hours away in Central and Eastern Washington. Ironically, Woodinville falls geographically within the Puget Sound AVA, yet virtually no one there uses local grapes. It’s a foreign concept to the Stoeckleins. “We live in our vineyards,” says Christine matter-of-factly.

With relatively few producers scattered over such a large area, it’s impossible to make generalizations about the region as a whole, which most say is a huge positive. “We love being the underdog region: There’s more room to innovate, more room to surprise people, and more satisfaction in the reaction when someone realizes their assumptions about Washington were completely wrong,” says Bayernmoor’s Harris. “Puget Sound is still being defined—and that’s a great thing to be a part of.”

YEAR AVA ESTABLISHED: 1995
TOTAL ACREAGE: 5.5 million
PLANTED ACREAGE: 121
NUMBER OF COMMERCIAL WINERIES: About 20 ELEVATION RANGE: 200 to 800 feet

Bet You Didn’t Know

Puget Sound is actually a huge glacial fjord system made up of deep underwater valleys, carved out by glaciers during the last Ice Age.

title: The Wine Industry Is Forgetting About an Important Generation
summary:
As wine sales dip, it benefits anyone who cares about wine to reevaluate how we talk to and about each other.

The post The Wine Industry Is Forgetting About an Important Generation appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
It should come as no surprise that a group nicknamed “the forgotten generation” is routinely ignored

Born between 1965 and 1980, Generation Xers are used to shrugging in the shadows. Members of the wine industry spend countless hours debating how best to attract and retain Millennials and Gen Z, and love comparing them to their Boomer predecessors. Meanwhile, Gen Xers are rarely mentioned. Their spending habits and side parts don’t inspire think pieces or TikTok memes, either.

It all raises questions about who wine professionals pay attention to and why. As wine sales dip amid social and economic headwinds, it benefits anyone who cares about wine to reevaluate how we talk to and about each other—and who gets left out of the conversation.

Some of it comes down to numbers. There are approximately 65 million Gen Xers in America, versus 74 million Millennials and 76 million Boomers at their peak.

While Xers are surrounded by more influential behemoths, they’re hardly lightweights. Members of Generation X are expected to drive consumer spending to $23 trillion by 2035, according to NielsenIQ. “If Gen X were a country, it would be the world’s second-largest consumer market, spending twice as much as China’s consumers,” Wolfgang Fengler and Marta Cyhan Bowles wrote in an article for the World Economic Forum last September.

Those purse strings reach all the way to the bottle shop. Gen Xers “punch above their weight in terms of wine spending and frequency,” says Liz Thach, MW, former president of the Wine Market Council (WMC). “Gen X is the largest purchaser of luxury wine in the United States.”

According to the WMC, 35% of Gen Xers buy wine that costs between $50 and $99 at least once a year. Only 25% of Boomers and 29% of Millennials do the same.

Given these figures, it’s puzzling how few wine businesses seem to court this demographic. For instance, last year, Gallo acquired Whiny Baby, a label focused on Gen Z, for an undisclosed sum. In 2024, when Browne Family Vineyards expanded its Do Epic Sh*t line to include bubbles and bourbon, a spokesperson credited the brand’s momentum to its resonance with “a broad audience, including the new wave of adult beverage enthusiasts like Gen Z.” If similar investments have been made in Gen X-centric wine projects, those headlines are few and far between.

“I definitely think Gen X needs more attention,” Thach says. Wineries could offer loyalty clubs akin to those of airlines to secure their relationships, she suggests. “Or try more targeted messaging: ‘You’ve made it, you arrived, you’re successful, and now you deserve this special wine.’”

Of course, we all contain multitudes. Even the best data points can’t encapsulate the diversity of groups with millions of members. Maybe the real question is whether dividing generational cohorts into diametrically opposed groups serves anyone in the long haul.

Identifying someone as a Gen Xer, Millennial, or member of Gen Z can be useful shorthand for explaining their preferred communication styles or predilections for ankle socks. But relying too much on labels can also flatten the idiosyncrasies that make people—and wine—so much more compelling than even the cleverest catchphrases or memes.

Besides, with culture wars occupying so much oxygen in and beyond the wine world, what’s the harm in giving each other a little room to breathe?

title: Wine Co-ops Have Always Been Essential. Now, They’re Becoming Excellent
summary:
The best co-ops today are zooming out and rethinking the overall structure of their business, allowing them to prioritize quality over quantity.

The post Wine Co-ops Have Always Been Essential. Now, They’re Becoming Excellent appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • Historically focused on volume over quality, wine co-ops provided vital economic stability for independent farming families.
  • Today, modern co-ops prioritize excellence by incentivizing high quality and adopting sustainable, site-focused farming methods.
  • This collaborative approach yields precise, terroir-driven wines that offer exceptional value for consumers.

For most of the 20th century, wine cooperatives produced bottles that were widely considered affordable and somewhat reliable, but rarely compelling. Much of that reputation came as a natural byproduct of their role: to absorb excess fruit from growers who hadn’t bottled their own wine, prioritizing volume and stability over distinction.

However unglamorous, that function was vital. In many regions, especially lesser-known ones, co-ops are the backbone of local winegrowing, allowing families to keep farming their land and remain independent from bigger brands.

So, what changed? Over the past few decades, a number of cooperatives have shifted from prioritizing moving volume to building value, focusing on less industrial vineyard work, refining approaches in the winery, and rethinking how growers are supported.

The result? Wines with real precision and a clear sense of place, often at prices far below what you’d expect. The biggest shifts haven’t necessarily been in the fields or cellars, but rather in the cultures and structures that surround them.

Consistency Over Character

The reputation co-ops had as efficient if unexciting workhorses wasn’t undeserved. Particularly in the postwar years, co-ops were built for survival, and growers were paid by volume, not quality. Grapes were pooled, blended, and processed centrally. Consistency was far more important than character.

“In the past, it was real,” David Jaegle, CEO of Cave de Ribeauvillé, says of the previous era’s quantity-over-quality approach. “The co-op produced a lot, fast… [there was] no need to make it good.”

That model worked, until it didn’t. Falling prices, changing consumer expectations, and a new generation of growers forced many to rethink co-op production and their roles in the global wine trade.

How Co-ops Are Changing

The best co-ops today operate on a different logic. By zooming out and rethinking the overall structure of their business, they can more easily prioritize quality.

At Domäne Wachau, for example, the growers aren’t suppliers, but owners. There are around 200 operations that farm tiny, fragmented plots across steep terraces, and each is responsible for their own parcels. Everything is harvested by hand, often down to micro-parcels, and vinified with a level of precision that rivals top estates.

“Top quality arises not despite the co-op structure, but because of it,” says Roman Horvath, MW, the Domäne’s winery director.

Alignment behind the single idea is key. Where they once lived off of volume, growers are paid here for quality instead. They share knowledge, resources, and risk. And crucially, they have a shared stake in the outcome.

In Piedmont, Produttori del Barbaresco has followed a similar path since its founding in 1958. “When you decide to make only Barbaresco, the quality path is the only path you’ve got,” says Aldo Vacca, the estate’s longtime director-turned-consultant. The co-op’s singular focus on one grape and one appellation has turned it into a benchmark for Nebbiolo, with cru bottlings that routinely outperform their price category.

In the Rhône, Cave de Tain shows what can happen when you scale up that philosophy. With nearly 250 growers, the cooperative could easily drift toward uniformity. Instead, it prioritizes caliber, insisting on parcel-by-parcel vinification and employing dedicated advisors to conduct thousands of annual vineyard visits. The goal is “not to do more, but to do better,” says managing director Ludovic Beau.

Across these co-ops, quality is built through education, collaboration, and constant dialogue. “Impose on me and I oppose; explain to me and I commit,” Beau says.

Farming, Not Just Winemaking

In the vineyard, quality-driven co-ops invest heavily in viticulture: lower yields, hand harvesting, cover crops, reduced chemical inputs, and site-specific farming. In Alsace, Zimmermann Thiébaut, president of La Cave du Vieil Armand, describes a “group effect,” where growers push each other toward better practices simply by seeing what’s possible next door.

It’s not always dogmatic. Organic certification is expensive and can be difficult in humid regions, so many co-ops opt for pragmatic sustainability instead. Many growers want “an escape route in case of emergency,” Vacca says. The result is often thoughtful, site-adapted farming rather than ideology.

And it shows in the wines. Thanks to the cumulative effects of better farming decisions over time, growers in regions worldwide report more balanced ripening, clearer site expression, and greater consistency.

The Economic Reality

There’s a less romantic truth behind all of this, however: quality only works if it sells.

“To bring everyone on board, it ultimately comes down to value,” Thiébaut says. “The only real judge is the final customer.”

Co-ops that have successfully repositioned themselves through better wines, clearer identity, and relentless communication, can reward growers accordingly. Those that haven’t remain stuck in the old cycle.

This is why the best co-ops feel focused. They know they won’t win on volume or price alone. Instead, they aim for credibility.

Ironically, while many collectors chase scarcity and allocation, some of the most intelligently made wines in Europe are coming from groups of growers working together.

The model might sound less romantic than stories of lone, intrepid vignerons, but it’s capable of accomplishing an important goal. When this collaborative system works, it aligns people, land, and economics in ways that individual estates often can’t. It can also turn larger areas toward responsible farming.

For those willing to look past the old stereotypes, that difference is exactly where the value is.

How to Spot Quality-Driven Co-ops

For drinkers, the upside is clear, but only if you know how to identify quality-driven co-ops. Here’s what to look for:

  • Single-vineyard or cru bottlings: This is a sign of parcel-level work, not bulk blending.
  • A tiered range: There are entry-level wines alongside more serious, site-driven bottlings.
  • Evidence of hand harvesting: This is sometimes mentioned on the labels, especially on premium cuvées.
  • Regional focus: The best co-ops are deeply rooted in one place, not spread thin.
  • A strong reputation in the trade: Sommeliers and importers tend to catch on faster than consumers. Find a trusted wine professional and follow them like a record label or a film director.
  • Prices that feel too low for the appellation: This is often the clearest signal.

title: Out West, This Underrated Wine Scene Is Finally Getting Its Due
summary:
Despite bordering two of the country’s most respected winemaking states, Idaho’s wine scene remains somewhat of a hidden gem—but not for long.

The post Out West, This Underrated Wine Scene Is Finally Getting Its Due appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Despite bordering two of the country’s most respected winemaking states, Idaho’s wine scene remains somewhat of a hidden gem. That doesn’t mean it’s a secret to the people who live in and around Idaho wine country, nor is it to the winemakers who have experienced industry-defying growth.

While it may not have the name recognition of its Pacific Northwest neighbors, like Oregon Pinot Noir or Washington Cabernet, Idaho wines are holding their own, racking up high scores at exceptional value. This year Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large Michael Alberty, who reviews wines from the state, awarded the Snake River Valley-based winery Telaya’s “fresh and floral” 2024 Grenache Blanc a 91—the first Grenache Blanc he had ever tasted from Idaho.

But the wine itself doesn’t tell the whole story of what makes Idaho wine so exciting. Take a quick visit to Telaya Wine Co.’s bustling riverside tasting room, a literal stone’s throw from the Boise River and a convenient bike ride from the city along the Boise Greenbelt, and you’ll get a sense of the playfulness, unpretentiousness, and outdoorsy spirit that makes Idaho wine tourism so hot right now. 

On the afternoon I visited, to my great surprise, I spotted people actually sharing bottles with friends, a social ritual I had thought was dying based on my experience in New York. Owner and winemaker Earl Sullivan stopped by my table and told me that Telaya had hosted four events the night prior. “The younger generation—they want to drink with an experience,” he said. It doesn’t hurt that the experiences are so easy—and affordable—to access: popular ones include “Rhythm on the River” live music nights, visiting food trucks with wine pairings, and monthly clothing swaps.

The Great Idaho Outdoors

The best way to experience Idaho wine is in Idaho, and not just because so many of its wines can only be purchased at the wineries themselves. It’s because the rolling hills, babbling brooks, and gorgeous sunsets of Snake River Valley AVA, just a 40-minute drive from the state’s capital, have blossomed into a mini Napa, minus the pretension and steep fees. Boise itself feels like a true wine country town, boasting its own urban wine trail and bustling tasting rooms. 

“Idaho offers wine lovers the perfect combination of stunning landscapes—hello, Hells Canyon—and excellent wineries making everything from Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon to Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc,” says Alberty. “If you are into outdoor activities like skiing, rafting, fishing, and rock climbing, Idaho needs to be your next wine destination.”    

Fueled in part by an enormous influx of wine-loving transplants from neighboring California, Washington, and Oregon during the pandemic, Idaho’s wine country growth is almost hard to believe in the context of broader industry struggles. According to Idaho Wines, the total economic impact of Idaho wine reached $314.1 million (which includes wine tourism), representing a roughly $64 million increase over previous five-year benchmarks.

Sullivan tells me that when Covid hit, the business grew 48%. “There’s a microtrend happening in the Valley,” he said. “There was an influx of so many people who have wine knowledge.”

Kerry Hill Winery owner Mindy Mayer, an extremely successful McDonald’s franchisee from Oregon, found herself in Idaho because she was on the hunt for a good sheepdog. Mayer purchased a farm in Wilder, located in the AVA’s scenic Sunnyslope area, as she trained for sheepdog competitions.

Her friends started bugging her to get into the wine business. “‘It’s Idaho’s turn,’ they told me,” she says. When a neglected 35-year-old winery went for sale near her farm, she bought it. 

Producing wines from estate grapes, including Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Petit Verdot, the winery is named after the black-and-white Kerry Hill sheep Mayer raises on the flower-covered property, which is expressly landscaped to attract and nurture pollinators, owls, bats, and raptors. It’s certified salmon-safe and bee-friendly. 

Like at many wineries in the Snake River Valley and Boise, events are flourishing. Kerry Hill’s annual “Sip and Sheer” is one of the winery’s most popular: guests enjoy wine on the lawn while watching live sheep shearing demonstrations. There’s always a food truck and live music, as well as local spinners and weavers.

“I thought, ‘Who the hell is going to watch sheep being sheared?’” Mayer says. “A lot of people, it turns out.” 

On Mother’s Day, the winery did over $1,000 in frosé sales and actually ran out of glasses. “We have such a great ambiance, and we have all the options,” she said, “including NA beers and ciders.” Of note, nearly half of Idaho wineries are women-owned (47%) with 1,300 acres planted and over 70 wineries and cideries. 

Unlike some other domestic wine countries, Snake River Valley offers a slew of serious outdoor activities, so visitors can take it easier on tastings and diversify their itineraries. With dramatic river canyons, wildlife sanctuaries, and waterfalls aplenty, the AVA is an outdoors destination in its own right—no wine interest (or budget) required. 

On the Urban Wine Trail

If the future of wine travel is accessibility and convenience, Boise has that part figured out, too. The city’s wine trail is approachable and easy-to-navigate, with all the wineries and tasting rooms accessible by bike or foot. 

Best of all, it also happens to intersect with the Boise Idaho Potato Trail. (Because Idaho is known for potatoes, remember?)

After tasting Mouverdre and Viognier at Scoria Vineyards’ downtown tasting room, I strolled a few minutes to the Boise Fry Company for a brief and wondrous French fry intermission. There, I could choose between four different varieties of daily-changing potatoes (red, gold, Russet, and sweet on the day I visited) in six different shapes (regular, homestyle, shoestring, or curly), not to mention an entire bar of flavored salts and off-beat ketchups, including a blueberry one. Appetizer devoured, I made my way over to the Basque Market for pintxos and a bottle of Txakolina in the city’s historic Basque neighborhood. Boise has one of the largest concentrations of Basque residents per capita in the United States, a history rooted in the late 1800s when the original Basque immigrants arrived in Idaho to work as sheepherders. 

When I returned to my hotel, the boutique Inn at 500 Capitol, the lobby was filled with rescue dogs, local bottles, and small bites for a very special “Yappy Hour.” I couldn’t imagine anything better.

title: And Just Like That… Sarah Jessica Parker Makes Jalapeño Wine
summary:
On this week's episode of the Wine Enthusiast Podcast, we couldn't help but wonder: what drew the 'Sex and the City' star to jalapeño Sauvignon Blanc? Listen in to find out.

The post And Just Like That… Sarah Jessica Parker Makes Jalapeño Wine appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Sure, most people know Sarah Jessica Parker for playing the shoe-obsessed, “can’t help but wonder”-ing lead of the hit show Sex and the City, but Carrie Bradshaw is just one role in Parker’s long list of endeavors. The Emmy and Golden Globe winner has found success in the worlds of Broadway shows, film and television production, and publishing. But this is the Wine Enthusiast Podcast, so we’re here to talk about wine.

In 2019, Parker began working with Rob Cameron and Tim Lightbourne of the New Zealand winery, Invivo & Co. Starting with a simple Sauvignon Blanc, their collaboration has since blossomed into a full line of wines, Invivo X, SJP, which also includes a Pinot Noir from New Zealand and a Provence Rosé. Recently, the team launched their Spicy Jalapeño White Wine made with Sauvignon Blanc and natural jalapeño extracts—the latest example of the brand’s eagerness to innovate and produce products that consumers are excited about.

Despite having learned a considerable amount about the industry over the years, Parker remains committed to making wine feel approachable, above all else. “It’s not for the rarefied, you know,” she says. “We try really hard to have an affordable bottle that’s really well made. It doesn’t have to be out of reach.”

We had the chance to sit down with Parker and Cameron and covered it all—from spicy Sauvy B to no-alc products, to SATC’s cocktail culture and Carrie Bradshaw’s wine preferences.

On Breaking Wine Rules

Sarah Jessica Parker: “I always thought there were a lot of rules about wine. You know, I never wanted to be handed the wine menu at a restaurant with friends, I was always like, ‘no, no, you do it, you do it, you must know more.’ There were wrong pairings and right pairings. Invivo—from its inception and before I was lucky enough to be a partner in the company in the way that I am—that was something that they very much wanted to dispel, and it’s one of the many things I’ve learned since I first met with Tim and Rob. It’s been really good for us to hang our hat on that because it’s liberated the wine for us in a lot of ways, to just say, ‘Sure, there are traditionally things that a Sauvignon Blanc goes with, but really it’s up to the customer to make their own rules.’

It’s just reinforcing over and over again that we’re not precious about our wine. We want the customer to dictate how they’re using it. And I think that’s sort of the culture of Invivo. It’s been so nice to be working alongside people who don’t have such a formal approach to the way to drink and enjoy your wine.”

On the Making of Spicy Jalapeño

Rob Cameron: “It occurred to me that actually, yeah, jalapeño and Sauvignon Blanc is not as nuts as it sounds. Back in the eighties and nineties, New Zealand’s Sauvignon Blanc, Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc, was gaining its fame and growing internationally very fast. The wines they were producing back then were very green, very herbaceous, full of methoxypyrazines—that was the buzzword of the nineties—and that jalapeño character was quite often used as a tasting note or descriptor of the wine. 

And then, over the years, our winemaking has changed, our viticulture changed, and we started pushing the style of Sauvignon Blanc to a much more tropical one. That kind of got a new wave of consumers excited about it, but in that transition we sort of lost the ability to make these very herbaceous green wines again. 

So we started messing around with adding fresh jalapeño, dried jalapeño, and then ultimately we came up with an essence of jalapeño flavor. We’d take the actual jalapeños and steep them in alcohol, and that alcohol would carry all of the lovely flavor and aroma and some heat. And then we’d add very sparing amounts of it to a specific Sauvignon Blanc. This really isn’t just ‘throw some in and it’s fine.’ No, no, the base wine needs to be a very specific profile for it to work. Otherwise, they do clash, because tropical Sauvignon and jalapeño together are not particularly good bedfellows. So it’s not like our SJP Sauvignon Blanc, which has more citrus and doesn’t quite work with the jalapeño character. So that’s as much of the challenge is actually preparing the essence itself. 

And then of course: how hot shall we make it? How spicy? And I think it’s been so well received. The beauty of it is that you put something out there and it becomes a conversation piece. Should it be hotter? Is it too much? And that instantly gets people talking about it, which is really fun.”

On What the Wine Industry Needs Right Now

RC: “Innovation really is key. Like what we’re doing with the Spicy and the Zero [Invivo’s new de-alcoholized Sauvignon Blanc], we’ve got to keep telling new stories and keep giving some fun learnings and pathways for our consumers to walk down. Eventually they’ll come back to the core of what we do as an industry which is make great wine. So we keep telling stories, you know, keep engaging with our consumers. That’s really, really important. 

The booze industry, the wine industry, gets a bit of a bad rap in terms of… people saying they’re not drinking anymore, but we don’t believe that. We just believe that, you know, we’ve just got to keep talking to people. Wine is such an amazing world to sort of dip your toe in, and the beauty of it is that you can enjoy it a little or you can go crazy and and really get lost inside this vast array of types, styles, countries, regions, producers. There’s so much story there. 

So, making it accessible but also sort of planting the seed of this mysterious sort of journey that you can go on. It’s a lifetime of love, to be honest, and we’re gonna just keep telling those stories.”

On ‘Sex and the City’’s Cosmopolitan Obsession

SJP: “I don’t know whether its origin, specific to the show, was part of the original columns that Candace Bushnell wrote for The Observer that became the book Sex and the City. So forgive me if that is the genesis.

I think Michael Patrick and Darren [Star] just recognized that people were drinking it in bars in New York City. It wasn’t a sort of signature of the city or of women gathering and having cocktails—they just started, if not writing it specifically in the script, when we were shooting scenes in a bar and we were meant to have a cocktail, that was the cocktail that they would have us be drinking. Because those cocktails were made by the prop department and they were just cranberry juice with a lot of water. That was it. And I don’t even think they… mostly, I don’t even think they had a twist in them, you know? 

I never had a Cosmopolitan for years, but people were always kind and, when I would go to a restaurant, I’d get sent a Cosmopolitan. A lot of times the gesture was so nice, but the drink was not great, so I didn’t know a Cosmopolitan could be great. Then one day I went to a restaurant and somebody sent me a Cosmopolitan and it didn’t look like that at all. It was murky, and it had a bit of citrus, like a bit of the pulp you could see within the body of the drink, and it had a twist in it, and I tasted it. And I was like, ‘This is a Cosmopolitan. This is a really great drink.’ 

Made by assured hands and great bartenders, the Cosmopolitan is a fantastic drink. So, I do drink Cosmopolitans now. I can’t make a Cosmopolitan, but I really, really love a Cosmopolitan. I don’t drink them in my home. I can drink my wine at my home much easier. So I think that’s the story, but I might be wrong. And if anybody else knows, feel free to correct me on the record.”

On Drinking and Gathering Culture in the ’90s vs Now

SJP: “When I’m stopped on the street by this younger generation, they talk about gathering, going to a bar or a club or restaurant, and they’re not gathering to drink, but they’re enjoying a cocktail. So I sort of feel as if that is consistent, that idea of gathering—whether you’re drinking or not—at a club, at a bar, at a restaurant, at one another’s homes, you know, in a park, on a rooftop. That all seems to be pretty stable to me, like, that has sustained. 

I don’t know what kind of drinking young women are doing specifically. My daughters are not of drinking age, so I’m not as informed, but I see it all the time, especially in summer. You see, you know, a gaggle gathered ‘round a table, and they’re having cocktails or not or whatever. So that kind of, it seems that kind of culture, that kind of gathering seems to be still very active.”

On Carrie Bradshaw’s Go-To Pour

SJP: “I think she’d have the Pinot Noir. I think she’d be a red wine drinker. I remember her drinking red wine in the past. Yeah, I think she’d be a Pinot Noir drinker and probably, in summer, a rosé drinker. 

RC: “Something sophisticated.”

SJP: “Yes, something really sophisticated. She didn’t drink a lot of wine actually, but she did have red wine with Big a lot. Yeah. I think he really liked red wine.”

RC: “Something expensive.“

SJP: “Something expensive, yeah.”

The Guests

Sarah Jessica Parker is an award-winning actress and producer who is best known for her role as Carrie Bradshaw in the hit show Sex and the City. Throughout her career, Parker has been featured in numerous movies and TV shows along with on- and off-Broadway plays. In addition to her involvement with Invivo X, SJP, Parker runs a publishing imprint, apparel company, and, as a longtime New Yorker, is deeply engaged with the New York City community. 

Rob Cameron has been making wine for longer than he hasn’t. Cameron launched Invivo & Co. with his childhood friend, Tim Lightbourne, in 2008. Over nearly 20 years, the company has grown into one of New Zealand’s most successful wineries with operations across the world. Cameron is constantly looking for new ways to innovate and engage with consumers.

We have a zero alcohol wine that’s already been really successful for us. That too is because there’s been more and more of a demand by the consumer, including our, you know, restaurants and whether it’s, you know, a bottle or by the by the glass, and our distributors, but also the consumer is more and more asking for that as an option, whether they’re people who just are not wanting to drink for a period of time or in fact people who are not drinkers and don’t consume alcohol. so that too has taken a while to get right. That’s a really hard one to get right, and we knew what was out there in the market and we didn’t love it, and you know Rob has taught me to have very, very high standards. So that’s there, I guess you could say that’s a trend, but I really think that’s just more of a consumer understanding that they can ask for things and have them not be just a drink of a summer but in fact a proper staple in their you know, in their wine fridge or whatever.

MW

I feel like that’s another example of a trend that has more staying power than just a trend. Totally cool to hear about that. I have one more hundred percent wine question for you guys. Do you have any sort of controversial wine like hot takes or just any general wine hot takes?

SJP

I don’t have any hot takes. No, I think that you know, the thing that I’ve, one of the many things I’ve learned is when I first met with Tim and Rob, I thought there were a lot of rules about wine and you know, I never wanted to be handed the wine menu at restaurant with friends, I was always like, “no, no, you do it, you do it, you must know more.” There were pairings and there were wrong pairings and right pairings. Invivo from its inception, before I was lucky enough to be a partner in the company in the way that I am, that was something that they wanted very much to dispel. It’s been really good for us to hang our hat on that because it’s liberated the wine for us in a lot of ways to just say, sure, there are traditionally things that a Sauvignon Blanc goes with, but really it’s up to the customer to make their own rules. 

So that’s not a hot take. It’s just reinforcing over and over again that we’re not precious about our wine. We want the customer to dictate how they’re using it. And I think that’s sort of the culture of Invivo and it’s been so nice to be working alongside people who don’t have such a formal approach to the way to drink and enjoy your wine.

MW

Totally. Yeah, I think one of the things that I always think about with wine and wine pairings is just like what am I in the mood to drink? What am I in the mood to eat? Those are really the most important things when thinking about it. And you can go the classic pairing route, but sometimes you just wanna drink something yummy and eat something yummy and that’s really what it’s all about. Okay, I have to ask a couple Sex and the City sort of questions. I couldn’t…

SJP

Mm-hmm. Yeah. Sure.

MW

Couldn’t hang up without doing that.

The Cosmopolitan is sort of Carrie’s signature drink. It’s very much associated with the show. Do you know anything about how the creators chose the Cosmopolitan?

SJP

Maeve, I should have the answer to that question. I think I’ve heard Michael Patrick King talk about it. I don’t know whether its origin specific to the show was part of the original columns that Candace Bushnell wrote for The Observer that became the book Sex in the City. So forgive me if that is the genesis.

I think Michael Patrick and Darren [Star] just recognized that people were drinking it in bars in New York City. It wasn’t a sort of signature of the city or of women gathering and having cocktails. And they just started, if not writing it specifically in the script, when we were shooting scenes in a bar and we were meant to have a cocktail, that was the cocktail that they would have us be drinking.

I didn’t really, because those cocktails were made by the prop department and they were just cranberry juice with a lot of water. That was it. And I don’t even think they mostly I don’t even think they had a twist in them, you know? 

I never had a Cosmopolitan for years. And people were always kind—when I would go to a restaurant, I’d get sent a Cosmopolitan. A lot of times the gesture was so nice, but the drink was not great, so I didn’t know a Cosmopolitan could be great. And then one day I went to a restaurant and somebody sent me a Cosmopolitan and it didn’t look like that at all. It was murky, and it had a bit of citrus, like a bit of the pulp you could see within the body of the drink, and it had a twist in it, and I tasted it. And I was like, this is a Cosmopolitan. This is a really great drink. I mean, made by assured hands and great bartenders, the Cosmopolitan is a fantastic drink. So I do drink Cosmopolitans now. I can’t make a Cosmopolitan, but I really, really love a Cosmopolitan. I can’t open a Cosmopolitan. I can’t have, I don’t drink them in my home. I can drink my wine at my home much easier. So I think that’s the story, but I might be wrong. And if anybody else knows, feel free to correct me on the record.

MW

Well, I like that. I like that story. Similarly, wine and going out in New York were a big part of, sort of, the social universe and the story of both Sex and the City and And Just Like That. If Sex and the City were made today following characters in their thirties, how do you think that might change the culture?

SJP

In terms of their social lives, you mean?

MW

Yeah, I guess like how the like drinking culture now would affect…

SJP

I wonder, I don’t have a definitive answer, but the show is surprisingly really, really popular with generations that are much younger than me, including you know, young women my daughter’s age and slightly younger actually. Now they are not of drinking age, so I don’t include them in this. But when I’m stopped on the street by this younger generation, they talk about gathering, going to a bar or a club or restaurant, and they’re not gathering to drink, but they’re enjoying a cocktail. 

So I sort of feel as if that is consistent, that idea of gathering—whether you’re drinking or not—at a club, at a bar, at a restaurant, at one another’s homes, you know, in a park, on a rooftop. That all seems to be pretty stable, to be like that has sustained. I don’t know what kind of drinking young women are doing specifically. My daughters are not of drinking age, so I’m not as, I’m not as informed, but I see it all the time, especially in summer, you see, you know, a gaggle gathered round table, and they’re having cocktails or not or whatever. So that kind of, it seems that kind of culture, that kind of gathering seems to be still very active. You can tell me.

MW

I’ll tell you, I don’t know if they ever left, but Cosmos are back. They’re very back.

SJP

That’s nice to hear.

MW

I just have one more quick question. I’d love to hear from both of you. Carrie was a cosmopolitan drinker. If she drank wine, what do you think her go-to glass would be?

SJP

I think she’d have the Pinot Noir. I think she’d be a red wine drinker. I remember her drinking red wine in the past. And I do think that yeah, I think she’d be a Pinot Noir drinker and probably, in summer, a rosé drinker.

RC

Something sophisticated.

SJP

Yes, something really sophisticated. She didn’t drink a lot of wine actually, but she did have red wine with Big a lot. Yeah. I think he really liked red wine.

RC

Something expensive.

SJP

Yeah, something expensive.

MW

Going back a little bit then. Just the wine industry in general, is there one thing or a few things that you guys think the wine industry needs right now? I mean, I don’t need to list the challenges and everything happening, but what do you think the industry needs right now?

SJP

What do you think?

RC

I think what we’re doing with the spicy and the zero, like innovation is really key. We’ve got to keep telling new stories and keep giving some fun kind of learnings and pathways for our consumers to sort of walk down and then eventually they’ll come back to the core of what we do as an industry which is make great wine. So we could keep telling stories, you know, keep engaging with our consumers. It’s really, really important. 

The booze industry, the wine industry gets a bit of a bad rap and in terms of people saying they’re not drinking anymore, we don’t believe that. We just believe that, you know, we’ve just got to keep talking to people and keep saying wine is such an amazing world to sort of dip your toe in, and the beauty of it is that you can enjoy it a little or you can go crazy and and really get lost inside this vast, you know, array of types, styles, countries, regions, producers.

There’s so much story there. So, making it accessible but also sort of planting the seed of this mysterious sort of journey that you can go on. It’s a lifetime of love, to be honest. And we’re gonna just keep telling those stories.

SJP

Yeah, I agree and that’s, you know, yet another lesson learned from working with Invivo. Tim and Rob keep repeating that it’s not for the rarefied, you know, that we try really hard to have an affordable bottle, but that’s really well made, that it doesn’t have to be out of reach. In terms of the dollars and that you can have a really gorgeous bottle of wine and it is really nice to gather around a table with a great wine with friends, with you know a well planned meal or a pizza. 

I think we just like you know keep repeating like Rob said the stories but also that it’s not formal, you know, that it can be yours and you don’t have to know a great deal to reach for a bottle of wine. And it’s such a nice gift to bring to people, to you know, to homes for those who drink. and we’ll just keep trying to produce that affordable bottle that’s really special and hopefully become part of people’s lives, which is such an honor.

MW

Said that so beautifully. Wine really is for everyone. I think you’re both doing a great job of making a product that makes that accessible to everyone.

It’s been so, so wonderful to talk with you both. I really appreciate your time. Thank you both so much. This has been so great.

SJP

Thank you so much, Maeve. Thanks for having us.

RC

Thank you.

MW

So, would you try Spicy Jalapeño wine? Or maybe, like Carrie, you’re leading the movement to bring Cosmos back while sipping some Pinot Noir on the side? We’d love to know! You can email us your comments and questions at podcast@wineenthusiast.com. Remember, you can subscribe to this podcast on Apple, Spotify, and anywhere else you listen to your favorite shows. You can also go to wine enthusiast.com backslash podcast for more episodes and transcripts. I’m Maeve Wade. Thanks so much for listening.

title: As If Tourists Needed Another Reason, the Algarve Is Now a Food and Wine Oasis
summary:
Innovative wines, fine dining, and breathtaking beaches are drawing visitors to Portugal's southernmost coast.

The post As If Tourists Needed Another Reason, the Algarve Is Now a Food and Wine Oasis appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Eat & Drink
  • Restaurante Noélia — Seafood-heavy cuisine in a fishing village served with friendly service.
  • Austa — Stylish all-day restaurant with its own vegetable garden and low-intervention wines.
  • Sul — Family run coffee-shop-slash-wine-bar serving small plates and natural wines.
  • Ocean — Two-Michelin-starred fine dining experience.
  • A Ver Tavira — New to the scene, one-Michelin-starred fine dining experience.
Wineries
  • atlas.land — Italian winemaker Filippo Pozzi crafts terroir-driven field blends from old vines.
  • Monte da Casteleja — Soon-to-be certified biodynamic estate led by Guillaume Leroux.
  • Morgado do Quintão — Family-owned estate with activities ranging from cooking classes to outdoor movies.
Activities
  • Salmarim — An artisanal salt producer that hosts visits.
  • Feito No Zambujal — A farm run by two brothers and known for their presunto ham.
  • Beaches — Praia da Falésia, Praia da Marinha, Praia do Camilo, and Praia de Cacela Velha are favorites while Praia do Amado and Praia da Cordoama are best for surfing.
  • Fariniente — Boat rental company with options ranging from hours-long tours to private chef dinners.
Stay
  • Bela Vista— Boutique property with amenities spanning Michelin-starred dining, spa offerings, and nearby golf courses.
  • Morgado do Quintão — Quaint guesthouses located on a sprawling vineyard.

Long before destinations like Lisbon, Comporta, and the Azores became Portugal’s tourism hot spots, there was the Algarve. Since the 1960s, Portugal has drawn sun-seeking Europeans to its southernmost coastline, adored for its perennially pleasant weather, family-friendly beaches, and craggy caves. The recent rise in visitors from further afield (remember when it felt like every American was heading to Portugal?) has moved developers to build the likes of grand resorts and pristine golf courses—add them to the litany of indulgences for which the region is beloved. And all this growth has led to an ongoing refinement of the region’s culinary scene. 

Long have there been classic tascas, or Portuguese tavernas, along the Algarve serving traditional seafood dishes like dourada grelhado (grilled sea bream) and arroz de marisco (rather like a brothy counterpart to Spanish paella). Now with a vast and expanding inventory of resorts comes the gift of fine dining addresses, some of which have earned Michelin stars (Portugal received its own dedicated guide only in 2024, separated from the old Michelin Guide España & Portugal). In the last few years, the area has also welcomed hotspots that fit in between, like hip wine bars and modern bakeries that specialize in more than just flaky cups of pasteis de nata. Even the Algarve’s winemaking has found a new set of champions, making oenotourism one of the newest ways travelers can explore the coast. 

Here’s what food and drink enthusiasts need to know about the Algarve, from the best bars to the best beaches.

Where to Eat and Drink

One of the most iconic restaurants in the area is Restaurante Noélia in the relaxed fishing village of Cabanas. Self-taught chef Noélia Jerónimo serves a menu featuring the stars of Portugal’s seafood-heavy cuisine, from hearty cataplanas loaded with fresh fish to crispy choco frito (fried cuttlefish). But there’s no need to even look at the menu for regulars like Jorge Raiado, who heads operations at Salmarim, an artisanal salt producer in nearby Castro Marim. “[Jerónimo] knows I love the green beans rice with loads of parsley and coriander to add freshness,” he says. One of the reasons Raiado has been a loyal guest at Jerónimo’s restaurant for ages is “the special touch that takes me to my grandma’s table.”

While Restaurante Noélia is known for traditional hospitality, newcomer Austa in Almancil, a town known for its white-washed buildings, brings a more contemporary edge to the dining scene. The stylish all-day restaurant has its own vegetable garden that supports chef Beatriz Olivença’s cooking. The selection changes constantly, but if you’re lucky the craveable plate of crispy puntillitas (baby squid) or the green asparagus with eggs will be on the menu. Co-owner David Campus’ Iberian wine list focuses on low-intervention producers, such as Tiago Macena in Dão or Mas Gomà in Spain’s Penedès region. 

For an exclusively Portuguese vinho hour, head to the town of Burgau—known for Praia de Burgau, a beach fenced by cliffs—and grab an outdoor perch at Sul, a family run coffee-shop-slash-wine-bar that opened two years ago. The food menu has savory-sweet toasted croissants stuffed with quince jam and sheep’s cheese as well as grilled Algarve prawns dressed in cilantro and chilies. The cellar is stocked with mostly Portuguese natural wines, like Viúva Gomes’ Malvasia Branco from Colares, just outside Lisbon, and a beach-ready pét-nat rosé from Peluda Vinhos, winemaker Mariana Pala’s wine project based in Mondim de Basto, in northern Portugal. 

Lovers of fine dining can choose from two-Michelin-starred Ocean in tiny Porches to one-Michelin-starred A Ver Tavira, in picturesque Tavira and one of the region’s newest darlings. Raiado of Salmarim also recommends Näperõn in the charming seaside village of Odeceixe. It’s led by chef Hugo Nascimento who cooked at Lisbon’s celebrated Tasca da Esquina. 

Raiado commends Nascimento’s attention to detail, and the way he extracts the purest flavor from every ingredient, whether it’s the sweet potato or the miso. The wine list here highlights every part of Portugal, from Niepoort in Douro to Arvad in Algarve—and throws in a little bit of Champagne too.

Wineries to Visit

Portugal has a rich oenological history, but not a lot of it has organically come out of this part of the country. But these days an array of local and foreign winemakers are taking Algarvean wine to new heights. 

Campus of Austa recommends making an appointment to meet Filippo Pozzi of atlas.land in the hilltop village of Aljezur. A native of Lake Como, Pozzi relocated to the Algarve because he wanted to surf in the morning before working on his wines in the afternoon. Today, according to Campus, Pozzi is among the most exciting vignerons in Portugal, “adopting century-old abandoned vineyards from locals” to make field blends that capture the terroir of the “wild Algarvian Atlantic coast.”

Another one of Campus’ local favorites is Guillaume Leroux at Monte da Casteleja in lively Lagos (the Portuguese one), which will soon be certified biodynamic. “His orange wine, named Branco, is one of the best Curtimenta in southern Portugal,” Campus says, referring to skin-contact wines.

Nearby, a 20-minute drive away in Lagoa, family-owned Morgado do Quintão has one of the bigger wine tourism operations in the area. You can come for a tasting of their Negra Mole and Crato Branco (varietals indigenous to the Algarve) along with lunch, do a cooking class, hang out for movies under the stars, or throw a wedding on the estate.

Things to Do

For more agritourism, hang out with Jorge Raiado at Salmarim to learn more about his handcrafted fleur de sel. If you’ve eaten at any of the top restaurants in Portugal, you’ve likely had his salt. Campus also suggests visiting Feito No Zambujal, a farm run by brothers Manuel and Rui Jerónimo in the easternmost point of the Serra do Caldeirão. They are famous for producing the country’s best presunto, Portugal’s answer to prosciutto and jamon.

“With a big enough group, Rui and his wife will cook a meal for you in his home, exclusively using products from the farm—homemade wine and aguardente included,” Campus says; you’ll need at least a crew of six to sign up for this experience. “For dessert, a tour of the smokehouse and pork-ageing cave offers a glimpse into where the magic happens.”

While in the Algarve, getting in the water is a must. The massive Praia da Falésia in Albufeira, known for its nightlife, is one of the most popular stretches of sand so it’s best to come early in the day to avoid the biggest crowds. Praia da Marinha is famous for its double-arch rock formations. Praia do Camilo near Lagos is also very picturesque with its dramatic rock tunnel that connects different sandy areas. Praia de Cacela Velha near unpretentious Quarteira is rarely super busy because it’s not the easiest to reach. You have to take a water taxi, but you can also walk there during low tide. Either way, the spacious, fine-sand beach is worth it. And if you surf, try the breaks at Praia do Amado and Praia da Cordoama in the west.

And what’s a Euro summer without a little boat action? Raiado recommends a five-hour day with Fariniente, which you can board in the historic town of Tavira. They’ll take you wherever you want in the Algarve, including the crowded waters around the Benagil Caves, limestone caverns with a cathedral-like dome-shaped ceiling with a round opening that lets in sunlight. They also offer the option of bringing a chef onboard, which means adding a tasty seafood feast and fantastic Portuguese wines to your excursion. Raiado is partial to Ortigão’s sparkling cuvée from Bairrada made of 100% Baga grapes. “On Fariniente, the ocean is ours,” he says. “But with some luck, the dolphins will follow.”

Where to Stay

Bela Vista, a 38-room Relais & Château property on the cliffs of Praia da Rocha in Portimão, has it all: a Michelin-starred culinary courtesy of João Oliveira’s Vista Restaurante, a sweet Spa by L’Occitane, and a coveted location near golf courses and beaches. The sophisticated Vista Bar, which looks to be cloaked in thousands of tiles, has one of the best cocktail menus in the Algarve too. Try the Deep Ocean, a gin-based drink that features seaweed and cilantro. First opened in 1918, Bela Vista is smaller than the sprawling resorts in the area, but that’s the charm: You get the amenities but not the crowds. 

If you’d like to stay at a wine estate, book one of the minimalist cottages (or the four-bedroom Main House) at Morgado do Quintão. There’s a languorous pace of life here, a milieu surrounded by vineyards and almond trees. For when the heat gets to be too much, every unit comes with a pretty pool, and there’s never a shortage of chilled wine.

title: The Future of American Wine Travel Is Less About Luxury and More About Ease
summary:
As more American wine travelers push back against appointments and high tasting fees, some wineries are meeting the moment with more relaxed vibes.

The post The Future of American Wine Travel Is Less About Luxury and More About Ease appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
During the last 15 years, most American wine travel followed a script: appointment-only tastings in hushed rooms you felt lucky to enter, and sweeping vineyards you rarely saw up close. It could be beautiful. But it could also be expensive, intimidating, and exhausting—the kind of so-called vacation that requires a spreadsheet and a hired driver.

But my most recent wine trip was nothing like that. Last spring, in Northern Michigan, I found myself drinking frosé in a lavender field at Brys Estate on the Old Mission Peninsula. Lake Michigan glimmered nearby. Earlier that day, I’d lingered over a conversation with the winemaker from Black Star Farms. Later, I wandered through Traverse City’s asylum turned funky town center, Grand Traverse Commons, before driving along blue-water overlooks that made me audibly gasp. 

The wines were serious. The feeling was not.

That fun, breezy energy may be exactly the point. As established wine regions grapple with softer demand and pushback against high fees, a different model of American wine travel is gaining traction. It is less about traditionally defined luxury and more about ease. For many modern travelers, that means access, warmth, beauty, good food, and good wine take center stage.

The numbers suggest more than a vibe shift. According to WineAmerica’s 2025 Economic Impact Study, Michigan wine country generated 1.73 million tourist visits annually, Virginia 2 million and Texas 2.64 million. Once niche destinations, these are now significant tourism economies built around wine and hospitality.

Traditional wine regions are recalibrating, too. According to Silicon Valley Bank data reported by the San Francisco Chronicle, roughly 16% of U.S. wineries lowered tasting fees in 2025, with Napa and Sonoma leading the charge. 

Next-generation wine travel destinations in Michigan, Virginia, and Texas aren’t trying to out-Napa Napa. By leaning into local differentiators that make them feel exactly like themselves, they’re finding and defining success on their own terms.

A Different Kind of Wine Country

Besides, no one would mistake Northern Michigan for Northern California.

Traverse City sits between the Old Mission and Leelanau peninsulas, where Lake Michigan helps create a cool climate that suits Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, and increasingly, sparkling wines.

Here, wine fits into a larger agricultural landscape. There are vineyards, but also cherry orchards, farm stands, beaches beyond dunes, breweries, and ambitious restaurants that prioritize local ingredients and communities.

Patrick Brys, whose family owns Brys Estate Vineyard and Winery, says travelers increasingly want products that feel authentic and rooted in a sense of place. “We wanted to create a completely unique Michigan wine experience,” he says. “Not like we’re transporting a chateau from France into Michigan.”

That’s why wineries in the region emphasize their differentiators. In addition to cooler temperatures and glacial soils, you can find only-in-Michigan ingredients like Traverse City cherries and local whitefish, as well as proximity to outdoor attractions along the lakeshores and trails of Sleeping Bear Dunes.  

Distinctiveness is important to Virginia’s growing reputation as a wine travel destination, too. When Wine Enthusiast named Charlottesville and the Monticello AVA its 2023 Wine Region of the Year, it helped bring wider attention, locals say. The Monticello Wine Trail includes more than 40 wineries, and the appeal extends beyond the glass. 

At Pippin Hill Farm & Vineyards, visitors can drink Cabernet Franc or Petit Manseng with a garden-driven lunch on the veranda, looking across the vines toward the Blue Ridge. The distinction is not simply swapping the Mayacamas for another mountain view. While Napa’s identity is closely tied to Cabernet Sauvignon, Monticello invites discovery through less expected grapes that have found a foothold in Virginia’s humid, variable climate, paired with working farms, Charlottesville’s food scene, and centuries of complicated American history.

At Eastwood Farm and Winery, visitors can drop in without a reservation for self-guided flights, lunch, live music, and even juice flights for kids. At King Family Vineyards, free Sunday polo matches unfold against the Blue Ridge foothills. That combination may be the new sweet spot for wine travel. 

More than 40 wineries are clustered around Charlottesville, allowing visitors to move easily between rural tasting rooms. The wines offer their own point of difference. Rather than being defined by one dominant variety, producers are finding regional character in grapes including Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Viognier, and Petit Manseng, varieties particularly suited to Virginia’s challenging growing conditions. The result feels less like a polished wine-country circuit and more like an evolving conversation between history, landscape, and a new generation of winemakers.

Then there is Texas, a wine region still capable of surprising people. The state has 617 wine producers and more than 14,000 acres of vineyards, according to WineAmerica. The Texas Hill Country AVA alone contains more than 100 wineries.

“The Texas Hill Country has everything wine travelers are looking for,” says Shelly Wilfong, wine educator, writer, and host of the This Is Texas Wine podcast, “including beautiful vineyards, award-winning wines, and warm hospitality.” 

Texas also challenges assumptions about warm-climate wine. Growers cultivate more than 75 grape varieties, including Tempranillo, Tannat, Vermentino, and Picpoul Blanc. 

In many parts of the region, wineries are easier to access and navigate than ones in far-flung wine destinations, too. Most visitors to the Hill Country stay in Fredericksburg or Johnson City and taste along Highway 290, where wineries are clustered close together. “In the Texas Hill Country, visitors can expect a warm Texas welcome,” Wilfong says.

What Wine Travel Means Now

That last part matters. Wine travel does not always need to lead with seriousness. Sometimes the best ambassador for a region is a good glass of rosé, a pretty view, and someone genuinely happy you showed up.

This does not mean luxury is over. There will always be travelers who want rare bottles, private tastings, and architectural drama. But luxury itself may be changing.

For many travelers, luxury now means not needing reservations six months in advance. It means tasting fees that feel reasonable, conversations with winemakers, and destinations where wine is part of a larger weekend rather than a performance of expertise.

Great Wine Experiences Belong… Everywhere 

Not every memorable wine experience requires a vineyard visit or guided, sit-down tasting. Sometimes it is simply a great meal, a great glass of wine, and an unexpected conversation in a place you never saw coming.

Northern Michigan, Virginia, and Texas are very different, of course. But what they share is a sense of accessibility, of making wine feel less like a test and more like a conversation.

In a difficult moment for the wine industry, that may be an advantage. If younger and more occasional drinkers are less interested in wine as a status symbol, regions that emphasize discovery and hospitality may be better positioned than they realize.

Back in Northern Michigan, on that lavender-scented afternoon at Brys Estate, I was thinking less about prestige and more about the light reflecting on the lake and the cold, pink drink in my hand.
